pairs.source_text: quod si tacuisset, tamen ego eram dicturus, deus, qui poteram planius. nam mihi Auxilio est nomen. nunc operam date, ut ego argumentum hoc vobis plane perputem.
pairs.question: Quis deus in Cistellaria Plauti argumentum fabulae spectatoribus eloquitur?
pairs.question_en: Which god recounts the plot of the play to the spectators in Plautus' Cistellaria?
pairs.derivation: The play's theatrical curiosity: a personified god named Auxilium delivers a delayed prologue (only after the opening scenes, grumbling that the tipsy old woman has already told half the story). Canonical literature-fact of the named play; one-name answer verbatim (mihi Auxilio est nomen).

pairs.source_text: bene valete et vincite virtute vera, quod fecistis antidhac; servate vostros socios, veteres et novos, augete auxilia vostra iustis legibus, perdite perduelles, parite laudem et lauream, ut vobis victi Poeni poenas sufferant.
pairs.question: Quos hostes victos poenas Romanis daturos esse Auxilium deus in fine prologi Cistellariae Plauti optat?
pairs.question_en: Which conquered enemies does the god Auxilium at the end of the prologue of Plautus' Cistellaria pray will pay the penalty to the Romans?
pairs.derivation: The famous patriotic aside that dates the play: the prologue-god urges the audience to destroy the foe 'that the vanquished Poeni may suffer punishment' — composed while the Second Punic War was still being fought. Historical fact embedded in the named play; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: fuere Sicyoni iam diu Dionysia. mercator venit huc ad ludos Lemnius, isque hic compressit virginem, adulescentulus, vi, vinulentus multa nocte in via.
pairs.question: In qua urbe fabula Plauti quae Cistellaria inscribitur agitur?
pairs.question_en: In what city is Plautus' play called Cistellaria set?
pairs.derivation: The setting declared by Auxilium's prologue: Sicyon, where the Dionysia were held and where the whole action takes place (adulescens hic est Sicyoni, 190). Anchored to the named play; one-place answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: fuere Sicyoni iam diu Dionysia. mercator venit huc ad ludos Lemnius, isque hic compressit virginem, adulescentulus, vi, vinulentus multa nocte in via.
pairs.question: Quibus ludis mercator Lemnius Sicyonem venerat, cum virginem nocte vinulentus compressit, ut Auxilium deus in Cistellaria Plauti narrat?
pairs.question_en: For which festival games had the Lemnian merchant come to Sicyon when, drunk at night, he assaulted the maiden, as the god Auxilium recounts in Plautus' Cistellaria?
pairs.derivation: The originating event of the plot is pinned to a named festival: the Dionysia of Sicyon, which drew the merchant from Lemnos to the games. Festival realia + plot fact; anchored to Sicyon and the Lemnian; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: illa quam compresserat decumo post mense exacto hic peperit filiam.
pairs.question: Quoto mense post vitium oblatum virgo Sicyonia in Cistellaria Plauti filiam peperit?
pairs.question_en: In what month after the assault did the Sicyonian maiden in Plautus' Cistellaria bear her daughter?
pairs.derivation: A number fact resting on the ancient tenth-month reckoning of pregnancy (lunar months): the child is born decumo post mense. Anchored to the Sicyonian maiden of the named play; one-number answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam ego illanc olim, quae hinc flens abiit, parvolam puellam proiectam ex angiportu sustuli.
pairs.question: Vnde lena in Cistellaria Plauti puellam parvolam expositam sustulisse se narrat?
pairs.question_en: From where does the procuress in Plautus' Cistellaria recount that she picked up the exposed baby girl?
pairs.derivation: The exposure-and-rescue fact at the root of the plot: the newborn was cast out in an angiportum (back alley) and 'taken up' (sustuli — the technical verb) by the old woman. Infant exposure is core ancient social realia; anchored to the lena + the play; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: ut eampse vos audistis confiterier, dat eam puellam meretrici Melaenidi, eaque educavit eam sibi pro filia bene ac pudice.
pairs.question: Cui meretrici lena puellam expositam in Cistellaria Plauti dono dedit educandam?
pairs.question_en: To which courtesan did the procuress in Plautus' Cistellaria give the exposed girl to bring up?
pairs.derivation: The foundling's foster-mother: the meretrix Melaenis, who raised her as her own daughter 'well and chastely.' Anchored to the named foster-mother + the play; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: quae saepe mecum mentionem fecerat, puerum aut puellam alicunde ut reperirem sibi, recens natum, eapse quod sibi supponeret. ... eandem puellam peperit quam a me acceperat, sine obstetricis opera et sine doloribus, ... nam amatorem aibat esse peregrinum sibi suppositionemque eius facere gratia.
pairs.question: Quid Melaenis meretrix in Cistellaria Plauti simulavit, ubi puellam expositam a lena accepit?
pairs.question_en: What did the courtesan Melaenis in Plautus' Cistellaria pretend when she received the exposed girl from the procuress?
pairs.answer_en: That she herself had given birth to her.
pairs.derivation: The suppositio: Melaenis passes the foundling off as her own newborn — a 'birth' without midwife or labor — to bind her foreign lover. The supposititious child is a named practice of ancient social life and a comedy staple; anchored to Melaenis; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: verum enim meretrix fortunati est oppidi simillima: non potest suam rem obtinere sola sine multis viris.
pairs.question: Cui rei meretricem simillimam esse lena apud Plautum in Cistellaria pronuntiat?
pairs.question_en: To what does the procuress in Plautus' Cistellaria declare a courtesan to be most similar?
pairs.derivation: The lena's proverbial simile on the meretrix's trade: like a flourishing town, she cannot keep her estate without many men. Quotable maxim of the courtesan-versus-matron speech; anchored to the play; two-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Matronae magis conducibilest istuc, mea Selenium, unum amare et cum eo aetatem exigere quoi nuptast semel.
pairs.question: Cuius mulieris esse lena in Cistellaria Plauti dicit unum virum amare et cum eo aetatem exigere?
pairs.question_en: For what kind of woman does the procuress in Plautus' Cistellaria say it is fitting to love one man and pass her life with him?
pairs.derivation: The famous mores contrast of the lena's speech: the matrona loves the one man she married once; the meretrix cannot. The one-man ideal (univira) is core Roman marriage morality, stated verbatim; anchored to the lena + the play; one-word answer.

pairs.source_text: Namque ecastor Amor et melle et felle est fecundissimus; gustui dat dulce, amarum ad satietatem usque oggerit.
pairs.question: Quibus duabus rebus Amor fecundissimus esse apud Plautum in Cistellaria dicitur?
pairs.question_en: In what two things is Love said in Plautus' Cistellaria to be most abounding?
pairs.derivation: The celebrated Plautine maxim on Love: fecund in honey and gall — a taste of sweet, bitterness heaped up to satiety. Quotable proverb with a checkable two-item point; anchored to the play; two-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Vtrumque haec, et multiloqua et multibiba, est anus.
pairs.question: Quibus duobus vitiis anum lenam Auxilium deus in Cistellaria Plauti notat?
pairs.question_en: With what two vices does the god Auxilium in Plautus' Cistellaria brand the old procuress?
pairs.derivation: The prologue-god's verdict on the drunken old woman who has just blabbed the plot: multiloqua et multibiba — the garrulous, bibulous anus, a stock figure of comedy here stamped in two coined words. Anchored to Auxilium + the lena; two-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Per Dionysia mater pompam me spectatum duxit. dum redeo domum, conspicillo consecutust clanculum me usque ad fores.
pairs.question: Quo spectatum Selenium mater per Dionysia duxerat, cum Alcesimarchus eam primum conspexit, ut ipsa in Cistellaria Plauti narrat?
pairs.question_en: What had Selenium's mother taken her to watch during the Dionysia, when Alcesimarchus first caught sight of her, as she herself recounts in Plautus' Cistellaria?
pairs.derivation: Festival realia: the Dionysia open with a pompa which respectable girls attend as spectators — and where lovers first see them (the classic New Comedy meeting). Anchored to Selenium + Alcesimarchus + the named festival; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: At ille conceptis iuravit verbis apud matrem meam, me uxorem ducturum esse:
pairs.question: Quid Alcesimarchus conceptis verbis apud matrem Selenii in Cistellaria Plauti iuravit?
pairs.question_en: What did Alcesimarchus swear in set form of words before Selenium's mother in Plautus' Cistellaria?
pairs.answer_en: That he would take Selenium as his wife.
pairs.derivation: The broken oath that drives the play: a formal oath (conceptis verbis — the technical phrase for a set-form oath) sworn before the girl's mother to marry her. Oath realia + plot fact; anchored to both named lovers; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: ei nunc alia ducendast domum, sua cognata Lemniensis, quae habitat hic in proxumo. nam eum pater eius subegit.
pairs.question: Cuiatem sponsam pater Alcesimarcho in Cistellaria Plauti invito ducendam subegit?
pairs.question_en: What bride did his father force upon the unwilling Alcesimarchus in Plautus' Cistellaria?
pairs.derivation: The rival match: the father compels a marriage with a Lemnian kinswoman living next door — the obstacle the recognition will remove. Anchored to Alcesimarchus + the play; two-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: postquam ille uxori iusta fecit, ilico huc commigravit; duxit uxorem hic sibi eandem quam olim virginem hic compresserat, et eam cognoscit esse, quam compresserat;
pairs.question: Quam feminam mercator Lemnius in Cistellaria Plauti, mortua priore uxore, Sicyone uxorem duxit?
pairs.question_en: What woman did the Lemnian merchant in Plautus' Cistellaria marry at Sicyon after his first wife died?
pairs.answer_en: The very woman he had once assaulted as a maiden.
pairs.derivation: The play's second knot: the Lemnian (Demipho) returns, and his new wife turns out to be the woman he wronged — mother of the exposed girl he now seeks. Canonical plot fact of the named play; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Credo ego Amorem primum apud homines carnificinam commentum.
pairs.question: Quid primum apud homines Amorem commentum esse Alcesimarchus apud Plautum in Cistellaria credit?
pairs.question_en: What does Alcesimarchus in Plautus' Cistellaria believe Love first invented among men?
pairs.derivation: The famous opening sententia of Alcesimarchus' lovesick monody: Love was the first inventor of the torturer's trade. Quotable maxim with one checkable point; anchored to the named speaker + play; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: ita pater apud villam detinuit me hos dies sex ruri continuos, neque licitum interea est meam amicam visere
pairs.question: Quot dies continuos pater Alcesimarchum ruri apud villam in Cistellaria Plauti detinuit?
pairs.question_en: For how many days on end did his father keep Alcesimarchus in the country at the farm in Plautus' Cistellaria?
pairs.derivation: A clean number fact: six unbroken days at the villa away from his beloved — the separation that opens the lover's lament. Anchored to Alcesimarchus + the play; one-number answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: quia nos libertinae sumus, et ego et tua mater, ambae meretrices fuimus: illa te, ego hanc mihi educavi ex patribus conventiciis.
pairs.question: Cuius condicionis se et Melaenidem esse lena in Cistellaria Plauti fatetur?
pairs.question_en: Of what status does the procuress in Plautus' Cistellaria confess that she and Melaenis are?
pairs.answer_en: Freedwomen, who had both been courtesans.
pairs.derivation: Social-status realia: the two old women are libertinae and former meretrices, raising girls got 'from chance fathers' — the demimonde milieu of the play stated plainly. Anchored to the lena + Melaenis; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nam hic crepundia insunt, quibuscum te illa olim ad me detulit, quae mihi dedit, parentes te ut cognoscant facilius. accipe hanc cistellam, Halisca.
pairs.question: Quid in cistella, unde comoediae Plauti nomen Cistellaria inditum est, conditum erat?
pairs.question_en: What was kept in the little casket from which Plautus' comedy takes its name Cistellaria?
pairs.derivation: The title-fact: the cistella holds the crepundia with which the baby was handed over, kept so the parents could recognize her more easily — the recognition-token apparatus that names the play. Anchored to the named play + Selenium; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Inter novam rem verbum usurpabo vetus: quod dedi datum non vellem, quod relicuomst non dabo.
pairs.question: Quod verbum vetus Melaenis in Cistellaria Plauti usurpat, cum Alcesimarcho amicam reddere negat?
pairs.answer: Quod dedi datum non vellem, quod relicuomst non dabo.
pairs.question_en: What old saying does Melaenis quote in Plautus' Cistellaria when she refuses to give Alcesimarchus back his beloved?
pairs.answer_en: 'What I gave I wish ungiven; what remains I will not give.'
pairs.derivation: A proverb explicitly flagged as such (verbum vetus) and quoted verbatim — the retort of the wronged party breaking off a relationship. Checkable point (which saying?); anchored to Melaenis + Alcesimarchus; answer is the proverb itself.

pairs.source_text: alibi quaere ubi iuri iurando tuo satis sit subsidi: hic apud nos iam, Alcesimarche, confregisti tesseram.
pairs.question: Quam rem Alcesimarchum apud se confregisse Melaenis in Cistellaria Plauti dicit, cum ei fidem denuntiat ruptam?
pairs.question_en: What does Melaenis in Plautus' Cistellaria tell Alcesimarchus he has broken at her house, declaring the bond of trust ended?
pairs.derivation: The idiom rests on real custom: hosts and friends kept a split tessera (hospitalis) as the token of their bond, and breaking it ended the relationship. Mores realia carried by every hearer; anchored to the named characters; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: itaque me Iuno regina et Iovis supremi filia itaque me Saturnus eius patruos— MEL. Ecastor pater.
pairs.question: Quis deus pater Iovis est, ut Melaenis Alcesimarchum perperam iurantem in Cistellaria Plauti corrigit?
pairs.question_en: Which god is Jupiter's father, as Melaenis corrects the wrongly-swearing Alcesimarchus in Plautus' Cistellaria?
pairs.derivation: The joke of the bungled oath assumes the canonical genealogy: Alcesimarchus calls Saturn Jupiter's uncle and is corrected — 'his father, by Castor.' Shared myth knowledge; anchored to the named gods and characters; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: ALC. Itaque me Ops opulenta illius avia— MEL. Immo mater quidem.
pairs.question: Quae dea mater Iovis est, ut Melaenis in Cistellaria Plauti Alcesimarchum eam aviam vocantem corrigit?
pairs.question_en: Which goddess is Jupiter's mother, as Melaenis in Plautus' Cistellaria corrects Alcesimarchus who calls her his grandmother?
pairs.derivation: Same bungled-oath joke, second correction: Ops opulenta is Jupiter's mother, not his grandmother. The Saturn-Ops-Jupiter genealogy is core Roman myth; anchored to the named deities; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: di me omnes, magni minuti, et etiam patellarii faxint, ne ego dem vivae vivos savium Selenio,
pairs.question: Qui di praeter magnos et minutos ab Alcesimarcho iurante in Cistellaria Plauti invocantur?
pairs.question_en: Which gods besides the great and the small are invoked by the swearing Alcesimarchus in Plautus' Cistellaria?
pairs.derivation: Religious realia in a comic oath: the di patellarii, the humble household gods who receive their offerings on little dishes (patellae) — a Plautine glimpse of domestic cult. Anchored to the speaker + play; two-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: vix exculpsi ut diceret, quia ei promisi dolium vini dare.
pairs.question: Quo praemio promisso Lampadio servus in Cistellaria Plauti anui persuasit ut rem de puella exposita eloqueretur?
pairs.question_en: With the promise of what reward did the slave Lampadio in Plautus' Cistellaria get the old woman to tell the story of the exposed girl?
pairs.derivation: The bibulous old woman again: her tongue is pried loose only by the promise of a whole dolium of wine. A checkable point playing on stock mores; anchored to Lampadio + the anus; two-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: ego te reduco et revoco ad summas ditias, ubi tu locere in luculentam familiam, unde tibi talenta magna viginti pater det dotis;
pairs.question: Quot talenta magna dotis patrem inventae filiae daturum Lampadio in Cistellaria Plauti praedicat?
pairs.question_en: How many great talents of dowry does Lampadio in Plautus' Cistellaria proclaim the father will give his recovered daughter?
pairs.derivation: A clean dowry figure: restored to her rich family, the girl would receive twenty great talents as dos. Marriage-property realia + number fact; anchored to Lampadio's speech + the play; one-number answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: non enim hic, ubi ex Tusco modo tute tibi indigne dotem quaeras corpore.
pairs.question: Quo more mulierem corpore sibi dotem quaerere Lampadio apud Plautum in Cistellaria dicit?
pairs.question_en: In what people's fashion does Lampadio in Plautus' Cistellaria say a woman earns herself a dowry with her body?
pairs.derivation: A famous testimonium of the Roman stereotype (already in Herodotus of the Etruscans): girls earning their dowry by prostitution is 'the Tuscan way.' Ethnographic mores fact; anchored to the named custom; two-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: MEL. Quis istic habitat? LAMP. Demipho dominus meus.
pairs.question: Quis senex dominus erat Lampadionis servi in Cistellaria Plauti?
pairs.question_en: Which old man was the master of the slave Lampadio in Plautus' Cistellaria?
pairs.derivation: The house identified by name: Demipho, the Lemnian who wronged Phanostrata and now hunts for the exposed daughter, is Lampadio's master. Anchored to both named characters; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Dico ei, quo pacto eam ab hippodromo viderim erilem nostram filiam sustollere. ... nam mihi ab hippodromo memini adferri parvolam puellam eamque me mihi supponere.
pairs.question: A quo loco urbis puella exposita sublata esse in Cistellaria Plauti memoratur?
pairs.question_en: From near what place in the city is the exposed baby girl in Plautus' Cistellaria recorded as having been taken up?
pairs.derivation: The exposure spot fixed by two witnesses (Lampadio saw the taking-up; Melaenis remembers the baby brought from there): beside the hippodromos, the racecourse of Sicyon. Place-anchored plot fact; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: vidi exeuntem mulierem. PHAN. Illam quae meam gnatam sustulerat? LAMP. Rem tenes.
pairs.question: Quae matrona in Cistellaria Plauti filiam olim expositam per Lampadionem servum quaerit?
pairs.question_en: Which married lady in Plautus' Cistellaria searches through the slave Lampadio for the daughter once exposed?
pairs.derivation: The searching mother of the play: Phanostrata (so named in the personae and scene-headings), Demipho's wife, whose exposed baby is Selenium. Anchored to the named slave + play; one-name answer.

pairs.source_text: Prius hanc compressit quam uxorem duxit domum, prius gravida facta est priusque peperit filiam; eam postquam peperit, iussit parvam proici: ego eam proieci, alia mulier sustulit, ego inspectavi.
pairs.question: Quis servus in Cistellaria Plauti puellam parvam iussus proiecit et quis eam tolleret inspectavit?
pairs.question_en: Which slave in Plautus' Cistellaria exposed the baby girl as ordered and watched who picked her up?
pairs.derivation: The exposure executed and witnessed by the same man: Lampadio cast the child out and spied on the woman who took her up — which makes the recognition possible years later. Anchored to the named slave; one-name answer.

pairs.source_text: postremo, quando aequa lege pauperi cum divite non licet, perdam operam potius quam carebo filia.
pairs.question: Cui cum quo aequa lege agere non licere Melaenis apud Plautum in Cistellaria queritur?
pairs.question_en: For whom against whom does Melaenis in Plautus' Cistellaria complain that it is impossible to contend on equal legal terms?
pairs.answer_en: For the poor against the rich.
pairs.derivation: The quotable sententia of the powerless: the poor cannot go to law with the rich on equal terms. Proverbial social maxim with a checkable two-term point; anchored to Melaenis + the play; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: quamne in manibus tenui atque accepi hic ante aedis cistellam, ubi ea sit nescio, nisi ut opinor loca haec circiter excidit mihi.
pairs.question: Quae ancilla in Cistellaria Plauti cistellam cum crepundiis ante aedes amisit?
pairs.question_en: Which maidservant in Plautus' Cistellaria lost the little casket with the tokens in front of the house?
pairs.derivation: The accident that resolves the play: Melaenis' maid Halisca drops the cistella while running to stop Alcesimarchus' suicide, and Lampadio finds it at the door. Canonical plot fact of the title object; anchored to the named maid; one-name answer.

pairs.source_text: sed is hac iit, hac socci video vestigium in pulvere, persequar hac.
pairs.question: Cuius calceamenti vestigium Halisca in pulvere in Cistellaria Plauti vestigans videt?
pairs.question_en: The print of what footwear does Halisca, tracking in the dust, see in Plautus' Cistellaria?
pairs.derivation: Dress realia in the tracking scene: the tell-tale footprint is of a soccus, the low slipper — proverbially the very shoe of comedy. Anchored to Halisca + the play; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Crepundia haec sunt, quibuscum tu extulisti nostram filiolam ad necem.
pairs.question: Quibus signis Phanostrata in Cistellaria Plauti filiam olim expositam recognovit?
pairs.question_en: By what tokens did Phanostrata in Plautus' Cistellaria recognize the daughter once exposed?
pairs.answer_en: By the childhood tokens (crepundia) found in the casket.
pairs.derivation: The recognition moment: the mother knows at sight the crepundia sent out with her doomed baby — the token-and-recognition practice attached to infant exposure. Anchored to Phanostrata + the casket; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: quot annos nata dicitur? HAL. Septemdecim. PHAN. Mea est.
pairs.question: Quot annos nata erat Selenium cum Phanostrata mater eam in Cistellaria Plauti agnovit?
pairs.question_en: How old was Selenium when her mother Phanostrata recognized her in Plautus' Cistellaria?
pairs.derivation: The clinching number of the recognition: the girl's stated age, seventeen, matches the count of years since the exposure (ut numerus annorum attulit). Clean number fact; anchored to both named women; one-number answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Imitatur nequam bestiam et damnificam. PHAN. Quamnam, amabo? LAMP. Involvolum, quae in pampini folio intorta implicat se: itidem haec exorditur sibi intortam orationem.
pairs.question: Cui bestiolae vitium vastanti Lampadio in Cistellaria Plauti mulierem intortam orationem exordientem comparat?
pairs.question_en: To what little vine-ravaging creature does Lampadio in Plautus' Cistellaria compare a woman spinning a twisted speech?
pairs.derivation: Agricultural realia in a simile: the involvolus, the pest that rolls itself up in the vine leaf — a creature every Italian farmer knew (Cato prescribes against it). Anchored to Lampadio + the play; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: CATERVA Ne exspectetis, spectatores, dum illi huc ad vos exeant: nemo exibit, omnes intus conficient negotium. ... nunc quod ad vos, spectatores, relicuom relinquitur, more maiorum date plausum postrema in comoedia.
pairs.question: Quis in extrema Cistellaria Plauti spectatores adloquitur et more maiorum plausum poscit?
pairs.question_en: Who addresses the spectators at the very end of Plautus' Cistellaria and asks for applause 'after the ancestral custom'?
pairs.derivation: Theater realia: the epilogue is spoken not by a character but by the caterva, the assembled company, telling the audience no one will come back out — the ending is settled indoors. Convention of the palliata; anchored to the named play; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: ubi id erit factum, ornamenta ponent; postidea loci qui deliquit vapulabit, qui non deliquit bibet.
pairs.question: Quid actori qui in agendo deliquit post fabulam fore caterva in Cistellaria Plauti spectatoribus nuntiat?
pairs.question_en: What does the troupe in Plautus' Cistellaria announce to the spectators will happen after the play to the actor who made mistakes?
pairs.answer_en: He will be flogged; the one who made none will get a drink.
pairs.derivation: A celebrated glimpse of the Roman acting company's discipline: once the costumes (ornamenta) are laid off, the erring player is beaten and the faultless one drinks. Theater realia stated verbatim in the epilogue; anchored to the play; short two-part answer verbatim.
